# Page 6^page=6
Arc length and the metric tensor

# Page 7^page=7
Our set-up Consider the coordinate system with basis e1, e2, e3 and corresponding coordinates x1, x2, x3. Let ds be the arc length between two in˝nitely close points xi and xi + dxi. Let the vector dr join the two points. dr has covariant components dxi and contravariant components dxi, that is, dr = dxie i and dr = dx iei. e1 e2 e3 xi xi + dxi e1 e2 e3 xi xi + dxi dr dx1 dx2 4 30

# Page 8^page=8
Arc length ds Arc length ds By de˝nition, we have (ds) 2 = |dr| 2 = dr · dr. Now, because dr = dxie i and dr = dxiei, we can write (ds)2 = ei dxi · ek dxk ︸ ︷︷ ︸ contravariant = gik dxi dxk, or (ds) 2 = e i dxi · e k dxk︸ ︷︷ ︸ covariant = gik dxi dxk. 5 30

# Page 9^page=9
Arc length ds - Part 2 Arc length ds We can also write (ds) 2 = e i dxi · ek dxk ︸ ︷︷ ︸ mix = dxi dxi because gi i = 1. Thus, we end up with the formulas (ds) 2 = gik dxi dx k, (ds) 2 = gik dxi dxk, (ds) 2 = dxi dxi. 6 30

# Page 10^page=10
Arc length and the metric tensor Arc length and the metric tensor These equations (ds) 2 = gik dxi dxk, (ds) 2 = gik dxi dxk, (ds) 2 = dxi dxi express the square of the element of arc length in the given coordinate system in terms of gik (or gik). The quantities gik (or gik) `determine the metric' of the given space and are known as the metric tensor : gik is the covariant metric tensor, gik is the contravariant metric tensor, g.k i is the mixed metric tensor. 7 30

# Page 11^page=11
Orthogonal Bases Orthogonal Bases Orthogonal bases are particularly important since the coordinate systems most commonly used in physics and applied mathematics are orthogonal. We now consider a basis e1, e2, e3 and its dual basis e1, e2, e3 to be both orthogonal . 8 30

# Page 12^page=12
Orthogonal Bases and the metric tensors Orthogonal Bases and the metric tensors For this orthogonal basis e1, e2, e3, we have gik = ei · ek = gki = e i · e k = 0 if i ̸= k. Thus, the general expansion of a vector A Ai = gikAk, and A i = gikAk reduces to the case i = k: A1 = g11A 1, A2 = g22A2, A3 = g33A3 A1 = g11A1, A2 = g22A2, A 3 = g33A3. Thus there is a simple relationship between gii and gii. 9 30

# Page 13^page=13
Orthogonal Bases and the matric tensors - part 2 Orthogonal Bases and the metric tensors We have A1 = g11A 1, A2 = g22A2, A3 = g33A3 A1 = g11A1, A2 = g22A2, A 3 = g33A3. In particular, A1 = g11A 1 implies A1 = A1 g11 , but also, we have A1 = g11A1. Thus, A1 g11 = g11A1 which implies g11 = 1 g11 . 10 30

# Page 14^page=14
Orthogonal Bases and the metric tensors - Formulas Orthogonal Bases and the metric tensors Conclusion: if e1, e2, e3 is an orthogonal basis, then g11 = 1 g11 , g22 = 1 g22 , g33 = 1 g33 . 11 30

# Page 15^page=15
Orthogonal Bases Orthogonal Bases Going back to our arc length equations (ds) 2 = gik dxi dx k, (ds) 2 = gik dxi dxk, (ds) 2 = dxi dxi, for i = k we can rewrite them as (ds)2 = 3∑ i=1(hi dxi)2, where the quantities h1 = √g11, h2 = √ g22, h3 = √g33 are called the metric coe˚cients . 12 30

# Page 16^page=16
Example Example In a system of Cartesian coordinates x1, x2, x3 with orthonormal basis i1, i2, i3, the element of arc length is given by (ds) 2 = gjkdxjdxk = ij · ikdxjdxk = δjkdxjdxk in terms of δjk. In other words, (ds) 2 = 3∑ i=1(hi dxi) 2 = (dx1) 2 + (dx2)2 + (dx3) 2, and the metric coe˚cients satisfy h1 = h2 = h3 = 1. 13 30

# Page 17^page=17
Finding the basis vectors Finding the basis vectors We can determine the basis vectors from the position vector r. On the one hand, we have seen that (ds)2 = |dr|2 = dr · dr = (ei dx i) · (ek dxk) = (ei · ek) dxidxk. On the other hand, (ds) 2 = |dr| 2 = dr · dr = ( ∂r ∂xi dxi) · ( ∂r ∂xk dxk) = ( ∂r ∂xi · ∂r ∂xk ) dxidx k. Therefore the basis vectors are ei = ∂r ∂xi . 14 30

# Page 18^page=18
Finding the basis vectors - Part 2 Finding the basis vectors Since the basis vectors are ei = ∂r ∂xi , the metric tensor is gij = ei · ej = ∂r ∂xi · ∂r ∂xj = ∂rℓ ∂xi ∂rℓ ∂xj , where r = (x1, x2, x3) are the Cartesian coordinates of r. 15 30

# Page 19^page=19
Summary: Orthogonal Bases, the Metric Tensor and Arc Length Summary Orthogonal coordinate system (x1, x2, x3) and position vector r. Basis vectors ei = dr dxi . The metric tensor is given by gik = ei · ek ̸= 0 if i = k. The arc length is then (ds)2 = gikdx idxk = ei · ekdxidx k = 3∑ i=1(hidxi)2, where the metric coe˚cients are hi = √gii = √ei · ei. 16 30

# Page 20^page=20
Example Example In cylindrical coordinates (x1, x2, x3) = (r, θ, z), we have the position vector r is given by r = r cos θ i1 + r sin θ i2 + z i3 where i1, i2, i3 are the usual Cartesian basis vectors. The basis vectors are then e1 = ∂r ∂r = cos θ i1 + sin θ i2 e2 = ∂r ∂θ = −r sin θ i1 + r cos θ i2 e3 = ∂r ∂z = i3. 17 30

# Page 21^page=21
Example - Part 2 Example The basis vectors are e1 = cos θ i1 + sin θ i2, e2 = −r sin θ i1 + r cos θ i2, e3 = i3, and the metric tensor is gij = ei · ej = 0 if i ̸= j because the system is orthogonal . We can ˝nd the arc length element (ds)2 = gijdxidxj = g11dx1dx1 + g22dx 2dx2 + g33dx3dx3. 18 30

# Page 22^page=22
Example - part 3 Example The basis vectors are e1 = cos θ i1 + sin θ i2, e2 = −r sin θ i1 + r cos θ i2, e3 = i3. The metric tensor is g11 = e1 · e1 = cos 2 θ + sin2 θ = 1, g22 = e2 · e2 = r2 sin 2 θ + r2 cos2 θ = r2, g33 = e3 · e3 = 1. The arc length element is then (ds)2 = gijdxidxj = g11dx1dx1 + g22dx2dx2 + g33dx3dx3 = (dr) 2 + (rdθ)2 + (dz) 2. 19 30

# Page 23^page=23
Example - Part 4 Example We have shown that the arc length element is (ds)2 = (dr)2 + (rdθ) 2 + (dz)2 = 3∑ i=1(hi dxi) 2. Thus, h1 = 1, h2 = r, h3 = 1. 20 30

# Page 24^page=24
Practical Question Your turn! In spherical coordinates (x1, x2, x3) = (r, ϕ, θ), we have the position vector r is given by r = r sin ϕ cos θ i1 + r sin ϕ sin θ i2 + r cos ϕ i3. Find the basis vectors and the metric coe˚cients. 21 30

# Page 25^page=25
Tensors - Preliminaries

# Page 26^page=26
Scalars, Vectors, and Tensors Scalars, Vectors, and Tensors Today, we will focus on Cartesian coordinate systems. Scalars and vectors are special cases of a more general mathematical object known as a tensor . As we discussed in the ˝rst lecture: 1. A scalar is a rank 0 tensor, representing a single value (e.g., temperature at a point). 2. A vector is a rank 1 tensor, representing a quantity with both magnitude and direction (e.g., velocity). 3. A 3 × 3 matrix is a rank 2 tensor, which can represent more complex relationships (e.g., the moment of inertia in mechanics). 4. And so on. 22 30

# Page 27^page=27
Scalars, Vectors, and Tensors - Part 2 Components In 3-dimensional space , we have: 1. Scalars have one component, e.g., λ ( 30 = 1 component). 2. Vectors have three components, e.g., v = (v1, v2, v3) ( 31 = 3 components). In general, a 3D tensor has 3n components, where n is the rank of the tensor. Remark: Higher Dimensions More generally, in m-dimensions, an m-dimensional tensor has mn components, where n is the rank of the tensor. 23 30

# Page 28^page=28
Formal definition of a vector Formal de˝nition A vector is a quantity satisfying: v′ i = Lijvj. That is, a vector is a quantity which transforms in a certain way under a rotation of coordinates. Transformation (rotation) matrix Lij The matrix Lij has the special property LT = L−1. This allows us to show Lij(Ljk)T = LikLkj = δik. 24 30

# Page 29^page=29
Formal definition of a vector - Part 2 Formal de˝nition We also have shown that x′ i = Lijxj, which implies Lij = ∂x′ i ∂xj . Next steps In this chapter we want to extend this de˝nition to a more general class of objects, which are called tensors . 25 30

# Page 30^page=30
Definition: Tensor De˝nition A quantity is a tensor if each of the free su˚ces transform in a certain way under rotation of the coordinates. For instance, Rank 2: T ′ ij = LimLjnTmn, Rank 3: T ′ ijk = LimLjnLkpTmnp, Rank 4: T ′ ijkℓ = LimLjnLkpLℓqTmnpq, etc. Note that on the RHS m, n, p and q are repeated dummy indices (summed over), and i, j, k, and ℓ are free indices. Thus, the equation balances. 26 30

# Page 31^page=31
Definition: Rank De˝nition The rank or order of a tensor is the number of free indices. Example A 3 × 3 matrix M is written as Mij with two free indices i and j which act as row and column counters. Thus, Mij is a second-rank tensor. Remark A tensor may have any number of free indices. For instance, a rank 7 tensor Pijkℓmnp transforms via: P ′ ijkℓmnp = LiaLjbLkcLℓdLmeLnf LpgPabcdef g. 27 30

# Page 32^page=32
Practical Question Your turn! Write down the transformation rule for: 1. a tensor of rank four, 2. a tensor of rank six. 28 30

# Page 33^page=33
Example: Kronecker Delta Example: Kronecker Delta The Kronecker Delta δij is a second-rank tensor. To show this, we must show δ′ ij = LikLjmδkm. In fact, recall that LikLjk = δij. Thus, LikLjmδkm = LikLjk = δij. Since δij is de˝ned in the same in any coordinate system, δij = δ′ ij. Thus, LikLjmδkm = δ′ ij. 29 30
